power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: We acknowledge the contribution of Dipl.-Statistikerin Nadine Bonberg, who assisted with the estimation of the sample size required for the study.
ChatGPT (OpenAI) was used to assist with language editing and to improve the readability of the manuscript.
All scientific content, interpretations, and conclusions were generated, reviewed, and verified entirely by the authors.
Lengthy examinations and motion artifacts remain major limitations of MR. 1, 2 Reducing scan time may improve patient comfort and decrease motion-related artifacts.
text.formatted: Lengthy examinations and motion artifacts remain major limitations of MR. <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2</ref> Reducing scan time may improve patient comfort and decrease motion-related artifacts.

text.text: To address these challenges, advanced acceleration techniques are now widely available on recent clinical scanner generations. 3, 4 Parallel imaging (PI) methods such as Generalized Autocalibrating Partially Parallel Acquisition (GRAPPA) and Controlled Aliasing in Parallel Imaging Results in Higher Acceleration (CAIPIRINHA) have reduced scan times across various MRI sequences. [5] [6] [7] [8] More recently, CS has emerged as an additional acceleration strategy based on undersampled MR data acquisition and iterative reconstruction, enabling reduced scan times or improved spatial resolution. 9 However, achievable acceleration with CS is limited by potential image quality degradation and the occurrence of reconstruction-related artifacts. 10, 11 MRI is the gold standard in the diagnostic work-up of MS, with high-resolution isotropic 3D-FLAIR serving as a key sequence for lesion detection and disease monitoring. 12, 13 Owing to its intrinsic sparsity and long acquisition time, 3D-FLAIR is particularly well suited for CS-based acceleration. 9 Prior studies have shown that compressed-SENSE accelerated 3D-FLAIR reduces scan time while maintaining image quality and may additionally allow increased spatial resolution in routine clinical brain MRI. [14] [15] [16] CS-accelerated 3D-FLAIR in MS cohorts has mainly been studied at 3T, demonstrating substantial scan-time reduction with preserved diagnostic image quality. 17 Most studies were conducted at 3T and rely on vendor-specific (PHILIPS) compressed-SENSE implementations, limiting generalizability.

text.text: Evidence comparing CS with established PI techniques such as GRAPPA or CAIPIRINHA at 1.5T remains scarce, and, to our knowledge, CS-accelerated 3D-FLAIR for MS lesion assessment has not yet been systematically evaluated at 1.5T in direct comparison with conventional PI methods.

This prospective noninferiority study compared optimized CS-and GRAPPA-accelerated 3D-FLAIR in clinical routine, using manual lesion count as the primary endpoint and aspects of image quality as well as automated lesion count and volume as exploratory secondary endpoints.
We followed the STARD and CONSORT reporting guidelines.
This single-center prospective non-inferiority study was approved by the institutional ethics committee of Carl von Ossietzky Universität, Oldenburg, Niedersachsen, Germany (registration no.
Sample size was estimated from a pilot retrospective analysis of routine clinical MRI data.
Written informed consent was obtained from all participants in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
No contrast agent or sedative medication was administered for study purposes.
However, patients who received contrast agents and/or sedation for clinical reasons were eligible.

During the first stage, sequence parameters for newer (CS, CAIPIRINHA) and conventional (GRAPPA) acceleration techniques were optimized in five healthy participants using a pragmatic empirical approach (see supplementary material).
Based on expert consensus, the best-performing sequence from each acceleration arm was selected for the clinical phase (Table 1).
text.formatted: Based on expert consensus, the best-performing sequence from each acceleration arm was selected for the clinical phase (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: During the second stage, the previously optimized best CS-accelerated and GRAPPAaccelerated sequences were added to routine clinical MRI examinations of patients with known or high clinical suspicion of MS, as indicated by neurological referral information.
Both sequences were acquired natively, although the overall protocol included contrast administration.
The acquisition order of CS and GRAPPA was systematically alternated.
The . subsequent comparison included an assessment of general and specific aspects of image quality as well as lesion load, counted both manually and automatically.

The primary endpoint was manual lesion count, with the primary hypothesis that optimized CS-accelerated FLAIR would not result in a clinically relevant reduction in counted lesions (>10%) compared with GRAPPA-accelerated FLAIR.
text.formatted: The primary endpoint was manual lesion count, with the primary hypothesis that optimized CS-accelerated FLAIR would not result in a clinically relevant reduction in counted lesions (>10%) compared with GRAPPA-accelerated FLAIR.

text.text: Secondary endpoints included comparison of overall image quality (numerical rating scale), general image artifacts (numerical rating scale), motion artifacts (numerical rating scale), SNR and CNR (numerical rating scale and ROI-based measurements), lesion delineation (numerical rating scale), as well as automatic lesion count and volumetry.
During sequence optimization, 5 healthy volunteers (≥18 years) were recruited.
Based on the  A CS acceleration factor of 6.4 was applied, resulting in a scan time of 4:00 min:s.
For GRAPPA-accelerated FLAIR, a GRAPPA factor of 4 was used, resulting in a scan time of 5:52 min:s (31.8% scan time reduction).
Both 3D-FLAIR datasets were acquired in the sagittal plane.
Detailed imaging parameters are summarized in Table 1.
text.formatted: Detailed imaging parameters are summarized in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>.

text.text: Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS Version 30 (IBM, Armonk, NY, USA) and SAS ® Analytics Software Online Studio (SAS Institute, Cary, NC, USA).
Standard descriptive statistics were applied.
Non-inferiority of CS relative to GRAPPA for the primary endpoint (manual lesion count) was assessed separately for each rater using log-transformed scores.

This was done using a one-sided t test with a prespecified non-inferiority margin of 10%, a difference considered clinically irrelevant for overall diagnostic performance. 19 Results were visualized using boxand-whisker plots.
text.formatted: This was done using a one-sided t test with a prespecified non-inferiority margin of 10%, a difference considered clinically irrelevant for overall diagnostic performance. <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19</ref> Results were visualized using boxand-whisker plots.

text.text: Non-inferiority was concluded if the lower bound of the one-sided 95% confidence interval for the mean difference (CS -GRAPPA) exceeded the predefined margin.
Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05.
text.formatted: Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05.

text.text: Secondary exploratory endpoints were summarized for each variable as median (interquartile range).
Visual comparisons of secondary endpoints were performed using split-violin plots to explore potential determinants of the main result (primary endpoint).

Interrater agreement between rater A and rater B for both CS and GRAPPA for all endpoints was reported as single-measure intraclass correlation coefficient derived from a two-way mixed-effects model with absolute agreement.
Initially, 72 patients with known or clinically suspected MS were recruited and provided written informed consent.
One patient was excluded because he had been enrolled twice during a follow-up examination.
Two patients did not undergo MRI because the examination was cancelled by the treating physicians after consent had been obtained, and one patient was excluded due to severe motion artifacts.
This resulted in a final study cohort of 68 patients.
The mean age of participants was 40.1 ± 13.3 years, and 42 patients (61.8%) were female.
The mean body mass index (BMI) was 26.1 ± 5.89 kg/m².
Most patients were diagnosed with MS (n = 36, 52.9%), whereas in 32 patients (47.1%) the initial clinical diagnostic suspicion was not confirmed after a mean follow-up period of seven months.
CS accelerated-FLAIR was non-inferior to GRAPPA-accelerated FLAIR, with no greater than 10 % reduction in manual lesion count for both Rater A p < .0001 and Rater B p = .005 (Figure 1).
text.formatted: CS accelerated-FLAIR was non-inferior to GRAPPA-accelerated FLAIR, with no greater than 10 % reduction in manual lesion count for both Rater A p < .0001 and Rater B p = .005 (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">1</ref>).

text.text: Interrater agreement for lesion count was excellent for CS-accelerated FLAIR and very good for GRAPPA-accelerated FLAIR (Table 2).
text.formatted: Interrater agreement for lesion count was excellent for CS-accelerated FLAIR and very good for GRAPPA-accelerated FLAIR (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref>).

text.text: The vertical dashed line on the far left indicates the non-inferiority margin (10%) obtained after logarithmic transformation of the mean differences between the two sequences.
The diamond on the horizontal arrow represents the mean difference.
Inferiority was rejected for both Rater A and Rater B, as the lower confidence limits (left-sided whiskers of the one-sided 95% confidence interval) lay well above the non-inferiority margin.
Subjective image quality ratings for CS-and GRAPPA-accelerated FLAIR are summarized in Table 3 and Figures 2 and 3.
text.formatted: Subjective image quality ratings for CS-and GRAPPA-accelerated FLAIR are summarized in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">3</ref> and Figures <ref type="figure">2</ref> and <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">3</ref>.

text.text: Median scores were high across all subjective parameters for both acceleration techniques, with substantial overlap in score distributions between methods and raters.
Rater A did not show a significant preference between methods, except for motion artifacts, which were rated slightly poorer with GRAPPA than CS.
In contrast, Rater B showed a slight preference for CS across all subjective image quality measures.
Inter-rater agreement ranged from moderate to good across metrics, with higher agreement for GRAPPA-accelerated FLAIR, particularly for overall image quality and lesion detection.
Because these secondary endpoints are exploratory, results were summarized descriptively with assessment of interrater agreement and no non-inferiority testing was performed.

text.text: MS diagnosis and treatment escalation decisions rely on frequent MR monitoring, with current MS imaging guidelines recommending 3D-FLAIR in the initial diagnostic work-up and during follow-up. 12, 13 Several acceleration techniques have emerged to speed brain imaging, reducing motion artifacts and scan times, particularly important for patients requiring frequent follow-up, such as those with MS. 8, 9, 20 CS and parallel imaging techniques can significantly reduce MR scan times without compromising diagnostic performance, across various clinical applications, including neuroradiological. [14] [15] [16] [17] Prior studies support the feasibility of CS-acceleration in neuroimaging, despite variability in machine vendors, field strengths, and acceleration factors.

text.text: However, the optimal balance among acceleration factor, scan-time reduction, and image quality remains debated. 14, 16, 17.
text.formatted: However, the optimal balance among acceleration factor, scan-time reduction, and image quality remains debated. <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17</ref>.

text.text: Molnár et al. 14 , Vranic et al. 15 and Mönch et al. 16 demonstrated that CS-accelerated 3D-FLAIR substantially reduces scan-time while maintaining image quality comparable to conventional acquisitions, with Mönch et al. additionally reporting improved spatial resolution. 16 However, Vranic and Molnár used PHILIPS vendor-specific compressed-SENSE implementations at 3T, whereas we evaluated a SIEMENS CS approach at 1.5T, limiting direct comparability.
text.formatted: Molnár et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14</ref> , Vranic et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15</ref> and Mönch et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16</ref> demonstrated that CS-accelerated 3D-FLAIR substantially reduces scan-time while maintaining image quality comparable to conventional acquisitions, with Mönch et al. additionally reporting improved spatial resolution. <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16</ref> However, Vranic and Molnár used PHILIPS vendor-specific compressed-SENSE implementations at 3T, whereas we evaluated a SIEMENS CS approach at 1.5T, limiting direct comparability.

text.text: The most comparable study, by Toledano-Massiah et al., compared CS-accelerated with nonaccelerated 3D-FLAIR in 23 patients with relapsing-remitting MS at 3T, demonstrating a 27% scan-time reduction with comparable image quality (SNR, CNR), lesion count, and automated lesion volume using a CS acceleration factor of 1.3. 17 We evaluated whether faster CS-accelerated 3D-FLAIR (factor 6.4; 4:00 min) preserved lesion detection relative to GRAPPA-accelerated 3D-FLAIR (factor 4; 5:52 min) in patients with known or suspected MS at 1.5T.
text.formatted: The most comparable study, by Toledano-Massiah et al., compared CS-accelerated with nonaccelerated 3D-FLAIR in 23 patients with relapsing-remitting MS at 3T, demonstrating a 27% scan-time reduction with comparable image quality (SNR, CNR), lesion count, and automated lesion volume using a CS acceleration factor of 1.3. <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17</ref> We evaluated whether faster CS-accelerated 3D-FLAIR (factor 6.4; 4:00 min) preserved lesion detection relative to GRAPPA-accelerated 3D-FLAIR (factor 4; 5:52 min) in patients with known or suspected MS at 1.5T.

text.text: CS achieved non-inferior manual lesion counts with excellent interrater agreement, corresponding to a 31.8% scan-time reduction without clinically meaningful loss in lesion detection, consistent with prior evidence. 17 Our study extends prior work by comparing CS with an optimized GRAPPA-accelerated reference, evaluating performance at the more widely available 1.5T, applying a prespecified non-inferiority margin to a clinically meaningful endpoint (manual lesion count), using a granular 0-100 image quality scale to capture subtle differences and including a larger cohort.

text.text: Although only 52.9% of participants had confirmed MS, all had lesions.
Subjective image quality parameters showed mild reader-dependent differences, with Rater B favoring CS and Rater A showing no clear preference except for slightly worse GRAPPA motion artifacts.
Moderate-to-good interrater agreement suggests these differences reflect individual preference rather than systematic differences between techniques. 21.
text.formatted: Moderate-to-good interrater agreement suggests these differences reflect individual preference rather than systematic differences between techniques. <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21</ref>.

text.text: Although ROI-based measurements showed higher SNR and CNR for GRAPPA-accelerated FLAIR, subjective ratings by Rater B paradoxically favored CS.
The difference between ROI-based SNR/CNR measurements in CS and GRAPPA may reflect differences in acceleration method reconstruction techniques.
CS relies on undersampled k-space acquisition, which reduces measured signal and increases effective noise.
However, the nonlinear iterative reconstruction suppresses incoherent noise, producing smoother background signal.
These effects are particularly pronounced in sequences such as 3D-FLAIR.

In contrast, GRAPPA utilizes coil sensitivity information and reconstructs missing kspace data, preserving signal and generally yielding higher SNR and CNR. 9, 22, 23 Thus, the lower objective SNR/CNR values in CS may primarily reflect signal reduction rather than increased noise because its reconstruction suppresses low-intensity signals while denoising.
text.formatted: In contrast, GRAPPA utilizes coil sensitivity information and reconstructs missing kspace data, preserving signal and generally yielding higher SNR and CNR. <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23</ref> Thus, the lower objective SNR/CNR values in CS may primarily reflect signal reduction rather than increased noise because its reconstruction suppresses low-intensity signals while denoising.

text.text: This creates visually "cleaner" images that may receive higher subjective ratings despite lower quantitative metrics, potentially explaining Rater B's preference.
The interrater discrepancy may reflect different perceptual sensitivities to image texture, noise, or overall image impression.
Therefore, subjective ratings do not necessarily align with purely mathematical relationships.

Rater B might have favored the smooth, denoised CS appearance, while Rater A equally weighted both techniques, illustrating that subjective ratings do not necessarily align with quantitative metrics. 21 Moreover, other MRI parameters might influence SNR and CNR.
text.formatted: Rater B might have favored the smooth, denoised CS appearance, while Rater A equally weighted both techniques, illustrating that subjective ratings do not necessarily align with quantitative metrics. <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21</ref> Moreover, other MRI parameters might influence SNR and CNR.

text.text: First, SNR is proportional to voxel volume and inversely related to the square root of receiver bandwidth.
Therefore, smaller voxels and higher bandwidth reduce measured SNR even when diagnostic performance remains acceptable.

This may partly explain the discrepancy, as our CS and GRAPPA sequences differed not only in acceleration method and factor but also in matrix and bandwidth, which can influence SNR and CNR independently of acceleration strategy. 24, 25 Second, quantitative noise and SNR/CNR measurements can be challenging.

text.text: when reconstruction extends beyond a simple Fourier transform.

Parallel imaging reconstructions (including GRAPPA) introduce spatially varying noise amplification, described by the coil geometry factor (g-factor), complicating conventional noise ROI measurements and making SNR comparisons sensitive to ROIs placement. 26, 27 Similarly, CS reconstructions are nonlinear and can alter the appearance and distribution of residual artifacts, often producing noise-like texture under incoherent sampling.

text.text: Consequently, the relationship between perceived image quality and measured SNR less straightforward than in fully sampled imaging. [28] [29] [30] [31] Automatic lesion counts and volumes were slightly higher in CS than GRAPPA, despite the lower SNR and CNR of CS acquisitions.

text.text: However, lesion conspicuity depends not only on global SNR and CNR but also on image texture, background noise distribution, and edge definition.
CS employs nonlinear iterative reconstruction with sparsity constraints, suppressing incoherent noise and smoothing homogeneous tissue while preserving structural interfaces.
This may improve lesion separation, increasing lesion detection.
9,11 Consequently, automated segmentation algorithms may identify lesions in CS images undetected in GRAPPA acquisitions, suggesting greater detection sensitivity.

However, this increased sensitivity may potentially come at the expense of specificity, as noise suppression and altered image texture may enhance subtle signal variations and cause them to be misclassified as lesions.
These may affect future AI-based image interpretation, as reconstruction techniques could influence automated detection performance.
Therefore, reconstruction methods should be considered when developing and validating automated lesion detection tools.
Automated MS lesion quantification tools are not yet standardized, and few studies have compared automated outputs across acceleration methods or with manual lesion counts.
The clinical relevance of lesions smaller than 3 mm remains debated, with the McDonald criteria.

considering only lesions of at least 3 mm in diameter. 12 The discrepancy between manual and automated lesion counts may partly stem from this issue, as manual assessment included lesions regardless of size, whereas automated segmentation and volumetric tools may be less sensitive to very small lesions.
text.formatted: considering only lesions of at least 3 mm in diameter. <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12</ref> The discrepancy between manual and automated lesion counts may partly stem from this issue, as manual assessment included lesions regardless of size, whereas automated segmentation and volumetric tools may be less sensitive to very small lesions.

text.text: We found higher automated lesion counts and higher volumes in CS-FLAIR than GRAPPA-FLAIR despite equivalent manual counts, suggesting reconstruction-dependent intensity distributions affect thresholding algorithms.

Whether automated lesion quantification tools can reliably replace manual counting using different acceleration methods remains unresolved and warrants caution, particularly in longitudinal assessments using varying acquisition techniques.

While automated approaches may offer a time-efficient complement to manual lesion counting, further research is needed to clarify method-specific differences, such as the types of lesions that may be missed by automatic volumetry in GRAPPA-acceleration or additionally detected in CS-acceleration.
In our study, CS-based volumetry identified more small and isolated lesions (Figure S1, supplementary material), although the clinical relevance of these differences requires further investigation.
text.formatted: In our study, CS-based volumetry identified more small and isolated lesions (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">S1</ref>, supplementary material), although the clinical relevance of these differences requires further investigation.

text.text: Toledano-Massiah et al. found no automated volume differences between CS-and conventional FLAIR at 3T, contradicting our findings, 17 potentially attributable to the different reconstruction families: CS vs.

text.text: GRAPPA as opposed to CS vs. conventional FLAIR, different field strengths (1.5 T vs.
3 T) and to the higher acceleration factors we employed in CS (6.4 vs.

1.3 in their study), with higher CS factors introducing greater intensity distribution changes and apparent lesion boundaries, factors known to influence artifact profile and affect automated thresholding.
Several limitations should be acknowledged.
First, only 52.9% of patients had confirmed MS, which may limit generalizability to lesion-rich patients.
However, all participants had at least two lesions, supporting applicability to patients with clinical MS-suspicion.
Second, the primary endpoint pooled all lesions rather than assessing lesion detection by anatomical . location.

Prior MS imaging studies stratified lesions by location, and the absence of this analysis may have obscured regional differences between sequences. 17 Future studies could assess the robustness of automated MS lesion detection across different acceleration techniques and vendors, particularly in longitudinal settings, where technical variability may influence perceived disease progression and treatment decisions.

text.text: AI-and deep learning-enhanced reconstruction combined with CS may further reduce scan time while preserving lesion detectability. [32] [33] [34] Ultrafast EPI-FLAIR also warrants further investigation for routine MS monitoring, alone or in combination with CS.
text.formatted: AI-and deep learning-enhanced reconstruction combined with CS may further reduce scan time while preserving lesion detectability. <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">[32]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">[33]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">[34]</ref> Ultrafast EPI-FLAIR also warrants further investigation for routine MS monitoring, alone or in combination with CS.

text.text: CS-accelerated 3D-FLAIR achieved noninferior lesion detection compared to GRAPPA with excellent interrater agreement and 31.8% shorter scans.
Despite higher objective GRAPPA SNR and CNR, subjective image quality was high for both techniques.

Automated volumetry yielded higher CS lesion counts and volumes, suggesting increased detection of small or isolated lesions, although their clinical relevance in longitudinal monitoring remains uncertain.
Overall, CS-accelerated 3D-FLAIR at 1.5T is a time-efficient, robust GRAPPA alternative.
